1.pericope_label: Naaman the leper, the captive maid’s word, and the letter that alarmed the king of Israel

schools.summary: Ellicott marks a break from what precedes, declines to fix the reign beyond saying it was a time of peace, glosses the name as a title of the sun-god, and draws attention to the high prophetic view that Jehovah, not Hadad or Rimmon, gives victory to Syria as well as Israel; he renders the clause as a brave warrior stricken with leprosy, notes the irony Thenius found in it that the victor over Israel must seek his only help in Israel, parses the maid’s wish as an exclamation, renders the gifts as holiday suits, and concludes that the total appears much too large and the numbers are probably corrupt. He also reads the rent clothes as at blasphemy, leprosy being a kind of living death, and asks why the king did not think at once of the prophet, answering that the two were not on good terms and that no miracle of this kind had yet been done. Keil and Delitzsch explain the idiom for receiving a man back from leprosy from the reception of Miriam into the camp, and take the figures of the present as they stand, judging the sum in keeping with the man’s position and not too great for the cure of a malady that would certainly prove fatal.

Henry holds that no man’s honour or valour can set him out of reach of the sorest calamities, there being many a sickly body under gay clothing, and that every man has some but that diminishes him, quoting Bishop Hall that the basest slave in Syria would not change skins with him; he presses that the prosperity even of those who do not know God must be ascribed to him, and that Israel should know that when the Syrians prevailed it was from the Lord. On the maid he makes the rule that the unhappy dispersing of God’s people has sometimes been the happy occasion of spreading the knowledge of God, and notes that no leper had yet been cleansed in Israel, so that she inferred the power from the other miracles and the willingness from his kindness. In the king’s alarm he sees both an affront to God and a design on himself, and says the fright came of misreading a letter well intended — it is charity to ourselves to think no evil — the king having made himself such a stranger to the prophet that the captive maid had Elisha more in her thoughts than he had.

Clarke reports that Jarchi and others identify the general with the man who drew the bow at a venture and killed Ahab, and finds it strange that Josephus passes him over when the history stands in the Chaldee, the Septuagint and the Syriac; he makes it a providential rule that God often permits great defects to accompany great eminence in order to hide pride from man; he infers pious parents for the maid and sets the goodness of providence against its severity, answering that if God allowed the parents to lose the child he did not allow the child to be without a guardian, and that by her captivity one of the most considerable families in Syria was brought to the knowledge of God; and he reckons the present at better than fourteen thousand pounds, calling it princely. On the king he has him reason from the maxim, held in Syria as in Israel, that God alone can cure the disease, and so infer a quarrel.
Gill has the king rend his clothes as at blasphemy, requiring of him what only God could do.

debates.question: Do the figures given for the present stand as written?

positions.view: They stand, and the sum is in keeping with the man’s position
The total appears much too large and the numbers are probably corrupt

debates.question: What did the king of Israel fear in the letter?

positions.view: Blasphemy, since it asked of him what only God can do
A quarrel deliberately sought, the impossibility of the request being the pretext
Both an affront to God and a design on himself, the fright arising from misreading a letter well intended

outliers.claim: Alone in remarking how strange it is that Josephus passes the whole history over, when it stands in the Chaldee, the Septuagint and the Syriac.
Alone in glossing the general’s name as a title of the sun-god.

9.pericope_label: The chariot at the prophet’s door, the order to wash in Jordan, and Naaman’s rage

schools.summary: Gill has the prophet retired as he commonly was, perhaps at prayer, and willing besides to show his contempt of worldly grandeur and to mortify the visitor’s pride; he takes the retinue for the man’s own grandeur and the prophet’s honour both.

Henry allows either reason for the prophet staying in, devotion he would not be diverted from or a lesson that before the great God all men stand on the same level; he turns the arrival into the posture of a suppliant, since those who showed prophets little respect at other times were complaisant enough when they needed them, and this one waited at the door as a beggar waits for an alms. He denies the washing was any means of cure at all, cold bathing being thought by some rather hurtful in a leprosy, so that it was a sign and a trial of obedience; and he finds in the scheme the man had laid the folly of pride, since he forgot that he was a leper, who ought not to stand on punctilios of honour, and a petitioner besides, and beggars must not be choosers.

Keil and Delitzsch rule out three explanations of the prophet’s staying indoors by name — the legal bar on dealings with lepers, which Ephraem Syrus assumes, fear of the leper, which Thenius suggests, and a wish to magnify the miracle, which C. a Lapide imagines — and put it down to the man’s own state of mind; they also explain why the flesh is said to return, the leprosy having turned it to festering matter. Ellicott returns to the avoidance of contact with a leper, noting that once cleansed the man goes in and stands before the prophet, and rejects the pride reading outright, holding with Thenius that there is no trace of pride about Naaman; he reads the plural as suggesting magnificence, will not have it with Bähr that the house was a hovel he disdained to enter, says the command itself made clear that no external application of the prophet’s was curing anything, and corrects the expected gesture to a waving of the hand toward the place, since the prophet would not touch what was unclean.

Clarke says the prophet had his orders from God and passed them on by a servant, calls the arrival preposterous on inspection — a leper sitting in state and affecting it — grants the water no tendency to remove the disorder and makes it a doctrine that the author of life and health may convey them by what means he pleases, and breaks the complaint into its four expectations of a personal visit, a standing attendance, a calling on the Name and a touch of the hand. Wesley makes the prophet’s silence partly a trial of faith and obedience, partly a point of honour for his religion, and puts the rage in four words: he supposed himself despised.

debates.question: Why did the prophet not come out to meet him?

positions.view: He was retired as usual, perhaps at prayer, and meant to mortify the man’s pride
Either devotion he would not be diverted from, or a lesson that all men stand level before God
He had his orders from God and simply transmitted them by a servant
Partly to try the man’s faith and obedience, partly for the honour of his religion
Not the legal bar on lepers, nor fear, nor a wish to magnify the miracle, but the man’s state of mind
To avoid contact with a leper; the pride explanation fails, there being no trace of pride about him

outliers.claim: Alone in calling the manner of the arrival preposterous on inspection, a leper sitting in state and affecting it.
Alone in reading the wait at the door as the posture of a suppliant, a beggar waiting for an alms.

12.pericope_label: Abana and Pharpar, the servants’ plea, and the sevenfold washing

schools.summary: Gill takes the first river from the marginal Amana and Mount Amana in Syria, equates it with the Chrysorrhoas of Pliny, and makes the second the Orontes that runs by the walls of Antioch, adding that no trace of either name survives and that the only river at Damascus now is the Barrady, which Maundrell describes dividing into three streams; he denies that the servants’ address is familiar or affectionate at all and makes it a term of honour and submission, rendering it my lord with the Targum.

Clarke will not identify the rivers at all, Maundrell having travelled the whole ground and found no vestige of the names, but supposes two branches of the Barrady must be meant; he answers the question whether the man might not wash at home with a flat no, since God had directed him to Jordan and by its waters or none should he be cleansed, the whole difference being that God will convey his influence by the one and not the other — a contention common enough among men, the Ganges bearing the bell in Bengal as the Thames does in England. He calls the address a title of the highest respect and affection, sets out the servants’ argument that what costs nothing should be done the more readily, and finds the scurf entirely gone and the flesh of a youth in its place. Wesley grants the rivers equal virtue as water and says what the man should have considered, that the cure was not to be wrought by the water but by the power of God; he reads the address as our father, spoken to show reverence and affection together.

Ellicott is confident of both rivers, the first being the present Burâda, the cold, descending from Anti-Lebanon through Damascus in seven streams, the second the Nahr el-Awâj, the swift, coming down from the great Hermon to pass south of the city, and he alone draws the contrast that gives the complaint its force, that both are clear mountain water where the Jordan is turbid and discoloured; he makes the point from the other end that if mere washing in a river were enough it were easy to do that at home and to much better advantage; he allows the address as a title but floats the possibility that the word is a corruption of the particle for if, which the Hebrew does not otherwise express; and on the number he quotes Keil for the covenant with Israel before setting beside it a parallel from the Assyrian exorcism texts. Keil and Delitzsch explain the seven as the stamp of the works of God.

Henry notes who delivered the reproof and makes it a mercy to have those about us who will tell us our faults though they are our inferiors; and he observes that the man was bidden to wash seven times and did but dip himself as many times, as lightly as he could, yet God so far honoured his own word as to make even that effectual.

debates.question: Which rivers are Abana and Pharpar?

positions.view: The Chrysorrhoas of Pliny and the Orontes that runs by Antioch
They cannot now be identified; two branches of the Barrady must be meant
The Burâda, descending from Anti-Lebanon, and the Nahr el-Awâj from the great Hermon

debates.question: What does the servants’ address to their master mean?

positions.view: A term of honour and submission, not of familiarity or affection
A title of the highest respect and affection
Our father, spoken to show reverence and affection together
Possibly not a title at all, but a corruption of the particle for if

outliers.claim: Alone in setting the sevenfold washing beside an Assyrian exorcism text of the age of Sargon of Agadê, in which a sick man is sent to bathe in the sacred waters at the mouth of the Euphrates.
Alone in illustrating the rivalry of rivers from Bengal, the Ganges bearing the bell there as the Thames does in England.

15.pericope_label: The confession, the refused present, the earth for an altar, and the house of Rimmon

schools.summary: Henry takes the confession for a noble one, which exposes the misery of the Gentile world since nations that had many gods really had none, and notes that the mercy of the cure moved the man more than its miracle, those being best able to speak of divine grace who have felt it. He denies that the prophet refused the present because he did not need it, being poor enough, or thought it unlawful, having taken presents from others: he would not have this Syrian able to say he had made Elisha rich. The request for earth he calls an over-doing to match the earlier under-valuing, the man who slighted the waters of Israel now over-valuing its earth, and likens the wish to asking a man for his picture. On the reservation he allows the plea might admit of some apology, yet turns it on the reader: a reservation for any known sin is a defeasance of the covenant.

Ellicott hears less in the confession than Henry does: like most contemporaries, Jewish as well as Syrian, the man believed in locally restricted deities, and in concluding that there is no god save in Israel he keeps that conception intact, which Ellicott calls a mark of historic truth in the account. He finds the request for earth natural to such a local idea of divinity, takes the reservation as a prayer for an unavoidable exception, apparent rather than real and not to be judged by a Christian standard, holds that the prophet as spokesman of Jehovah acceded to it, and identifies the god as the Assyrian thunderer of the air, identified with Hadad, of whom the tablets yield forty-one titles. Keil and Delitzsch have the prophet avoid all appearance of the selfishness that moved the false prophets, and hold that in answering Go in peace he neither approved nor disapproved what had been said, since no permission had been asked of him and without a special command he could only commend a new convert to God’s guidance; they note that most earlier theologians found a direct approval in the words.

Clarke holds that the Syrians might take a gift for payment of a cure God alone had worked; he rejects the altar reading of the two mules’ burden, asking why leave was needed for earth that could be lifted anywhere and how an altar could be built of two mules’ load carried to Damascus, and takes the burden for the silver and gold, called earth as others call gold thick clay, leaving the reader to choose. On the reservation he will not have the plea at all, holding that by no rule of reasoning can a man be asking pardon for what he may yet commit, since that would be the doctrine of indulgences, and reading the verbs in the past with Lightfoot so that the pardon sought is for bowings already done; he then reports a marginal note in one of De Rossi’s manuscripts directing that the word be read not rather than to him, on which the answer becomes a refusal. Wesley says the Syrians should see how God’s servants despised the wealth the prophets of the Gentiles sought so greedily, and asks what altar two mules could carry into Syria unless they were as large and strong as elephants.
Gill reports Jewish writers who have the man ask for soil from the prophet’s own house, conceiving a holiness in the ground he trod.

The silver and gold, called earth to show how little he now valued it

He neither approved nor disapproved, no permission having been asked of him
The question does not arise, the pardon sought being for bowings already done; and one manuscript reading would make the answer a refusal
Most earlier theologians found in the words a direct approval

outliers.claim: Alone in dismissing the altar reading by asking what altar two mules could carry into Syria, unless they were as large and strong as elephants.
Alone in identifying Rimmon as the Assyrian thunderer of the air, identified with Hadad, of whom the cuneiform tablets yield forty-one titles.

20.pericope_label: Gehazi runs after the Syrian, begs in his master’s name, and hides the spoil

schools.summary: Henry opens on the contrast, that the Syrian soldier had many servants and they were wise and good while the holy prophet has one and he proves a liar, and that those who heard of Elisha at a distance got good by it while the man who stood continually before him took no impression, for the means of grace cannot give grace. He calls the love of money the root of it and quotes Bishop Hall, that the man’s heart was packed up in the Syrian’s chests and he must run to fetch it; he anatomises the lie, which diverted to the servant the courtesy meant for the prophet and painted Elisha as a man who would say and unsay, swear and unswear; he calls the tale of two young scholars as silly as it was false, since if a token were wanted for two of them less than a talent might have served; he weighs what it risked, that the convert might have concluded the master kept his hands clean and sent others to make a gain of him; and he adds the sacrilege, the man hiding his gain as Achan hid his and then standing before his master ready for orders, none looking more observant and none more injurious.

Wesley makes the same opening point as Henry and in nearly the same words, that one would have expected a prophet’s servant to be a saint, yet the best ministers have often had about them those who were their grief and shame; he adds that the oath was sworn to give the deed a pretence, not considering that swearing to do a wicked thing does not excuse it but makes it worse, and notes that the gift was pressed on one who first declined it under a pretence of modesty. Clarke marks that the Syrian treats even a servant with the profoundest respect and renders his greeting as an asking after peace; he follows the Chaldee, Greek, Syriac and Arabic in making the hiding-place a secret or dark place, and draws the moral that a man doing a deed of darkness sought darkness to hide it in; and he supplies the weight that made two bearers necessary, each talent running to some hundred and twenty pounds.

Keil and Delitzsch have the Syrian spring down the moment he sees the servant running, in reverential gratitude toward the prophet, then press two talents on a man who had asked for one, sending two of his own servants to carry them ahead; they take the hiding-place for the well-known hill before the city. Ellicott finds the self-justification in the words themselves, the servant reasoning on the principle of spoiling the Egyptians; he calls the descent from the chariot an Oriental mark of respect and reads haste in the idiom, adding that the Syrian feared something had befallen the prophet; and on the place he allows either the rise on which the prophet’s house stood, where no window would have overlooked their approach, or a fortified hill among the defences of Samaria like the Ophel at Jerusalem, remarking that so particular a note of place is itself a note of historical truth.
Gill takes the hiding-place for a fortified post at Samaria with a watch, to whom the money could safely be committed.

debates.question: Where were the silver and the garments hidden?

positions.view: In a fortified post with a watch, where the money could safely be left
In a secret or dark place, the word being so rendered by the versions
On the mound of the city — the rise the prophet’s house stood on, or a fortified hill among its defences

outliers.claim: Alone in reading the servant’s self-justification as an appeal to the principle of spoiling the Egyptians.
Alone in catching the disproportion in the lie, that if a token were really wanted for two young scholars, something less than a talent of silver might have served.

25.pericope_label: The prophet’s discernment, the rebuke, and the leprosy that passed with the silver

schools.summary: Gill lays out three readings of the prophet’s question about his heart from the Jewish commentators: that his knowledge had not departed, so nothing could be hidden, which he credits to Ben Gersom; that his heart did not go with the errand, the deed being against his will, which he credits to Abendana; and the Targum’s, that the matter was shown him by a spirit of prophecy, to which he adds Maimonides. On the sentence he notes the exchange, that as through his covetousness the man had the money, so for his punishment he should have the disease.

Keil and Delitzsch will allow only one reading of the question — that the prophet’s heart had gone when the man turned from his chariot — calling it the only correct reading of words explained very differently elsewhere, noting that Theodoret and the Vulgate had given it already and that it agrees in sense with Thenius, who has the prophet present in spirit; they read the list of silver, clothes, oliveyards, flocks and slaves as the substance of the rebuke. Ellicott reaches the same sense and adds the point that makes it bite, that the prophet adopts his servant’s own phrase in severe irony, observing too that the English follows the Greek in supplying words the Hebrew lacks; he weighs a variant pointing which would yield a statement rather than a question, as the Greek, Vulgate and Arabic take it, but judges the Masoretic pointing much more suitable, and paraphrases the rebuke as asking whether that of all occasions was the time to yield to gain, when the man dealt with was a heathen who ought rather to have learnt not to confound the prophets of Jehovah with the diviners of the false gods; he takes the same list for a disclosure of what the servant meant to buy, and answers the objection that the sentence is too severe, holding that the prophet pronounces inspired judgment, that milder language might have left a false impression, and that covetousness and lying are never spared in Scripture.

Henry puts the rebuke sharpest, asking whether the man could find no better way of getting money than by belying his master and laying a stumbling-block before a young convert; and he reads the sentence as an exchange, that if he will have the money he must take the disease with it, so that a man contriving to entail lands entailed a loathsome disease instead.

Clarke says in a sentence that the man had the Syrian’s silver and should have the Syrian’s leprosy, and adds that the white spot appeared as the curse was spoken; on how long the curse ran he reports an opinion that descendants of his are leprous still, says Maundrell inquired in Judea and could not establish it, and calls it absurd, since the sentence held only until the posterity became extinct, which under such a disease must have come soon; and he closes by reading the whole chapter as a single providence, from the raid that carried off the girl to the healing and the conversion of the Syrian’s household, holding that what was severe to her parents was kindness to that family and that they lost their child only for a time, the frowning providence hiding a smiling face behind it, and drawing the lesson that without a religious education she could never have been the instrument of so great a deliverance. Wesley reads the phrase for ever as some generations and notes that the white sort of leprosy was reckoned by physicians the worst and incurable.
